uksc/2021/5.rationale: This is the leading UK Supreme Court authority, and indeed the definitive modern case, on whether ride-hailing (Uber) drivers are workers entitled to the national minimum wage and paid annual leave. It decides both the worker status question and the secondary "working time" question (that drivers are working whenever logged in, available and willing to accept trips), and also holds that contractual clauses purporting to preclude worker status are ineffective as unlawful attempts to exclude statutory rights. It is directly on point and would be cited first by any lawyer researching this question. All three highlights assist: [0] states the entitlement issue squarely; [1] records the Supreme Court's affirmation of the finding that drivers qualify for NMW, paid annual leave and other workers' rights; [2] identifies the NMW Regulations 2015 as defining working time for minimum wage purposes, which underpins the holding on when logged-in drivers count as working for NMW purposes.

ewca/civ/2018/2748.rationale: Uber BV v Aslam is the leading Court of Appeal authority, and indeed the starting point, on whether ride-hailing (Uber) drivers are 'workers' entitled to minimum wage and holiday pay. The judgment decided the drivers' appeals, remitting to the employment tribunal to determine the true contractual relationship using the statutory language in s.230(1)(b) ERA 1999 rather than the parties' labels (paras 34, 45-46), upholding the settlement agreement and remitting on status, with the claims at issue being unlawful deduction from wages for holiday pay, minimum wage and paid annual leave. The supplied paragraphs are the ET findings describing how the Uber system and Driver Addendum operate (paras 12-16) and the legal framework for characterisation (para 34), all directly relevant.

ewca/civ/2021/594.rationale: This is a leading Court of Appeal authority directly on the question. Addison Lee Ltd v Lange [2021] EWCA Civ 594 decided that the claimant Heathrow minicab (ride-hailing) drivers were 'workers' within limb (b) of s.230(3) ERA 1996 — the limb that carries entitlements to National Minimum Wage, holiday pay and working time rights — and that they were working whenever logged on. The judgment also applies Uber BV v Aslam and Autoclenz, holding that contractual clauses disclaiming any obligation to accept work do not displace the commercial reality, which is the same reasoning underpinning the NMW/holiday pay claims brought by gig drivers. It is squarely on point for a lawyer researching the question, and is itself part of the binding appellate line with Uber BV v Aslam [2021] UKSC 5. Grade 3.

eat/2024/162.rationale: This is a directly on-point EAT decision on the worker status of ride-hailing/black cab app drivers. The Employment Appeal Tribunal (HHJ Auerbach) applied the Uber v Aslam [2018] EWCA Civ 2748 control test to GT Gettaxi's driver app and held that the claimant driver was NOT a worker, distinguishing Uber on the basis that licensed London black cab drivers ply their trade on their own account, that fares are set by TfL rather than the platform, and that terms are imposed unilaterally. Because worker status determines entitlement to minimum wage (NMWA 1998) and holiday pay (WTR 1998), this is leading authority on precisely the question asked, and it also cites the earlier Johnson v Transopco UK Ltd [2022] EAT 6 outcome for the same driver under a rival app. All three quoted passages bear directly on the control analysis and the reasoning that determined the outcome.

eat/2022/6.rationale:
This is a leading Court of Appeal (Employment Appeal Tribunal) authority on whether an app-based (mytaxi black cab) driver is a 'worker' under s.230(3) ERA 1996 — the gateway question to entitlement to the National Minimum Wage and working-time holiday pay. The claim itself was for unlawful deduction, NMW non-payment and holiday pay, and the appeal turned squarely on worker status, applying Bates van Winkelhof and Windle to distinguish genuine independent contractors (own clients/customers) from limb (b) workers. It is directly on point for the substantive question and is routinely cited as the key UK appellate decision on gig/ride-hailing worker status.

Highlight assessment:
[0] The Bates van Winkelhof passage sets out the two types of self-employed person and the limb (b) worker test — this is the substantive legal test governing whether the driver is a worker, so it supports the answer (true).
[1] The finding that passengers contracted with the respondent and the driver delivered services under a separate contract with the respondent goes to the heart of the 'own client or customer' question; it is a central holding relevant to worker status and therefore to NMW/holiday pay entitlement (true).
[2] The T&C clause disclaiming any obligation to provide work through the app is a contractual term on availability only; it does not itself bear on minimum wage or holiday pay entitlement and merely shares context with the work-arrangement terms (false).

eat/2025/97.rationale: This is squarely the leading UK authority on the question. It is the Veezu litigation (509 private hire/ride-hailing app drivers), in which the claims are expressly for holiday pay, failure to pay the national minimum wage and failure to provide written statements of particulars, all resting on whether the drivers are workers or agency workers. The EAT (Popplewell J) sets up the preliminary issues hearing at which worker status, including multi-apping and 'at what times' questions following Uber BV v Aslam and the First-tier Tribunal decisions in Bandi and Afshar, will be determined. It is therefore the current go-to reference for how ride-hailing app driver status, and consequent NMW/holiday pay entitlement, is to be assessed in the UK. (It is a case management/procedural decision rather than a final ruling on status, but it is directly on point and the parent of the leading test.)

uksc/2018/29.rationale: This is the leading and directly on-point authority for the question posed: whether a tradesman who has been labelled a self-employed contractor (and invoiced with VAT) nonetheless qualifies as a limb (b) worker under s230(3) ERA 1996 and a s83(2)(a) Equality Act "employee", so as to bring a discrimination claim. The judgment decides precisely that issue on the facts of a plumber (Mr Smith) working exclusively for Pimlico Plumbers, holding him to be a worker. It is the case a lawyer would cite first.

eat/2026/109.rationale: The case is directly on point: Mathios Berhane v Adebowale Olujimi is an EAT appeal in which the sole issue was whether the Employment Tribunal had wrongly proceeded on the premise that the Claimant was, as asserted, a self-employed contractor, when in fact the Respondents' case was that he was an employee up to 30 April 2022 and thereafter a worker on a zero hours contract. The EAT held the ET erred in treating self-employed contractor status as an issue at all, and confirmed that worker status is sufficient to bring Equality Act 2010 discrimination claims. This is squarely the authority on a plumber (housekeeper here) being labelled/payed as a self-employed contractor yet claiming worker status in order to maintain a discrimination claim, and it also addresses the knock-on notice pay claim which requires employee status. eat/2025/23.rationale: The case is directly on point: the EAT appeal concerned whether a claimant who had been found to be a "self-employed independent contractor" (with a contract clause excluding employment) could nonetheless be a worker for the purposes of s.230(3), and the interaction of prior employment-status findings with the worker determination in a claim brought under the Equality Act. Paragraphs 48–50 hold that neither the "nothing in this agreement shall constitute a contract of employment" clause, nor findings and descriptions of the claimant as self-employed/independent contractor, nor his own self-descriptions, were automatically determinative of worker status, and the phrase "self-employed" is inherently ambiguous. Earlier paragraphs collect the governing authorities on the obligation of personal service (Ready Mixed Concrete, Byrne Brothers, Nethermere, Cotswold/Redcats integration and dominant purpose tests). This is a leading, squarely applicable authority on the question. All three quoted passages bear materially on it.

ewca/civ/2017/51.rationale: This is the leading Court of Appeal authority on precisely the question posed: whether a plumber engaged by a plumbing business under an agreement (and trade name/subcontracting arrangement) that labelled him self-employed was nonetheless a 'worker' under s.230(3) ERA / reg 2(1) WTR, and therefore an 'employee' for the purposes of s.83(2)(a) Equality Act 2010 disability discrimination claim. The appeal concerned exactly that issue (see [0]) and the ET's finding of worker status and 'employment' for the EqA purposes (see [2]). It is also the leading modern authority on the irrelevance of the contractual label of self-employment, and on substitution rights not necessarily taking a genuine self-employed contractor outside limb (b). Directly on point: grade 3.

eat/2023/2.rationale: Although the occupation here is a dentist rather than a plumber, the case is squarely on the legal question: an individual who contracted and was engaged expressly as a self-employed contractor, and who later asserted employee/worker status (with an Equality Act/unfair dismissal dimension), and how the status question is determined. Ter-Berg v Simply Smile Manor House Ltd [2023] EAT 2 is a leading EAT authority on (i) starting from the terms of the contract and the parties' intention, rather than immediately questioning whether the agreement delineates one of the three relationships, and only then the reality of the relationship if the terms do not match that intention; (ii) the personal service requirement derived from Ready Mixed Concrete, which applies equally to worker as to employee status; and (iii) expressly confirming at [47]-[48] that the Autoclenz/Uber approach applies to Equality Act 2010 claims, and that a worker-status claimant in a discrimination/unfair dismissal context faces no higher threshold. That is directly on point for the question posed.

eat/2022/6.rationale:
Johnson v Transopco UK Ltd [2022] EAT 6 is a leading EAT authority directly on the issue posed: whether an individual carrying on his own trade/business under a label of self-employment can nonetheless be a "worker" (s.230(3) ERA 1996 limb (b)) or an "employee" within the extended s.83 Equality Act 2010 definition in order to bring discrimination/employment claims. Although the facts involve a TfL-licensed cab driver rather than a plumber, the judgment contains the key modern analysis (post-Bates van Winkelhof, applying Windle) of the "client or customer" exception, and expressly holds that the s.83 Equality Act extension is subject impliedly to the same exception, making the two concepts a single body of guidance. It also usefully discusses Byrne Bros (the established-professions proviso, relevant because a plumber is not within a listed profession) and Pimlico Plumbers v Smith, which is the closest plumber authority. This is squarely a leading/directly on-point authority for a lawyer researching the question, not a tangential or coincidental hit.

Highlight assessment:
[0] Quoted passage from Bates van Winkelhof distinguishing the two kinds of self-employed person, and stating only the second is a limb (b) worker — directly states the test for a self-employed contractor claiming worker status. Supports.
[1] Passage confirming that the s.83 Equality Act 2010 extended "employee" definition is subject impliedly to the same "client or customer" exception as the worker definition — directly answers the discrimination-claim dimension of the question. Supports.
[2] Byrne Bros passage identifying the paradigm cases within the proviso (solicitor, barrister, accountant, architect) — useful in showing the exception is confined to established professions, i.e. why a plumber's self-employed label would not by itself defeat worker status. Supports.

ewca/civ/2018/2748.rationale:
The question concerns whether a tradesman labelled a self-employed contractor can nevertheless establish 'worker' status (and so bring an ET claim) — the classic label-versus-substance problem in s.230(3)(b) ERA 1996 cases. Uber BV v Aslam is the leading modern Court of Appeal authority on precisely that issue: it holds that s.230(3)(b) looks to the underlying reality of the bargain, not the parties' label, and sets out the multi-factor approach (ultimate question being the dominant purpose / essential nature of the contract, including whether the putative worker markets himself to the world as an independent business). Although the claims there were wages/working time/NMW rather than discrimination, the status analysis is directly transferable and controlling for any discrimination claim requiring worker status; para 9 also notes Uber accepted the WTR/ERA/NMWA apply 'provided they are workers as defined'. Grade 3.

Highlights: [0] states the dominant purpose test for identifying the essential nature of the contract — directly answers whether a self-employed label governs; supports. [1] identifies a specific factor (marketing oneself to the world at large as an independent) relevant to a plumber's genuine self-employment — supports. [2] is a bare citation to Autoclenz with no reasoning or test content; it shares subject-matter words but does not itself answer the question — does not support.

uksc/2022/34.rationale: This is the leading UK Supreme Court authority on precisely the question asked. It also confirms the transitional/orthodox position from West Mercia and Kinsela and explains the shift of the duty to creditors as a class on the onset of liquidation. This is directly on point and would be the first citation for a lawyer answering the question.

ewhc/ch/2016/1686.rationale:
BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana is the leading modern English authority defining the trigger for the creditors' interests duty: the duty arises where there is a real (not remote) risk that the transaction will put creditors' prospects of being paid at risk, and it does NOT require actual insolvency. This is directly and squarely on point for the question asked. While the case is best known for creditor-putting-risk / common law claim (and the wider jurisdictional discussion), paras 471-475 set out a thorough review of the case law on when the duty arises, including the articulation from Randall J in HLC Environmental that "established, definite insolvency before the transaction or dealing in question is not a pre-requisite for a duty to consider the interests of creditors to arise" and the Kalls/Vivendi formulation of "real and not remote risk". So grade 3.

Highlights:
[0] para 464, the concession that the duty can arise without actual insolvency — directly answers "at risk of insolvency" framing. Supports.
[1] para 465, a general methodological remark about statements of principle being expressed more broadly than warranted by the facts of the particular case; it is a case-management/weight point, not a statement of when the duty arises. Does not help answer the question. Does not support.
[2] para 471, note that Kinsela did not need to consider the degree of financial instability because the company was plainly insolvent — relevant to the boundary of when the duty bites (and helps distinguish the early cases, all involving actual or near insolvency). Marginally supports; it contributes to the picture of the trigger but on its own does not state the test. I'll mark it as supporting since it explains why the older cases don't define the threshold.

ewhc/ch/2026/1135.rationale: This judgment is squarely on the question asked. At [32]-[36] the court sets out the s.172 CA 2006 framework, restates the BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana SA [2022] UKSC 25 rule (creditor duty does not arise on a mere real and not remote risk of insolvency; requires imminent insolvency or probability of insolvent liquidation/administration; creditors' interests then carry appropriate weight and become paramount where insolvency is inevitable), records the divergent Supreme Court views on whether knowledge is required, applies Hunt v Singh [2023] EWHC 1784 (Ch) to a company already substantially insolvent (duty arises where directors know or ought to know there is at least a real prospect of an insolvency-related challenge failing), and explains the subjective/objective approach to breach of duty from PV Solar Solutions and Regentcrest. This is leading, directly on-point authority for a UK practitioner on the timing and content of the creditor duty, rather than a passing mention. Paragraphs 76-77 are unrelated (corporate benefit/EFRBS letterhead point) and were not highlighted.

ewhc/ch/2026/2184.rationale: This decision is squarely on the question asked. It applies Sequana to hold that, once a company is insolvent, the s.172 duty owed to the company extends to a duty to consider and not harm the interests of the company's creditors, and it finds an actual breach: the directors "at no time considered the interests of the creditors of the Company, other than SGL", obtained no valuation or legal advice, and made no attempt to identify how creditors would be paid if trading continued. It therefore illustrates both the trigger (the company being insolvent, at the date of the assignment and thereafter) and the content of the duty in a real application, making it a leading, directly on-point authority alongside Sequana itself. The other matched paragraphs (valuation evidence and s.241/IA 1986 issues) are off-point.

ewca/civ/2008/173.rationale: The question concerns whether a keeper (zoo) is liable for damage caused by an escaped animal — here a penguin damaging a neighbour's car. McKenny v Foster is squarely on point by close analogy: a farm keeper's cow escaped from a field, strayed onto the highway and damaged the claimant's car, and the Court of Appeal applied the Animal Health Act 1971 ss.2 and 8 — holding no strict liability under s.2(1) (cow not a dangerous species), and requiring knowledge of a causative abnormal characteristic under s.2(2)(b)/(c), while noting s.8 abolished the common-law restrictions on negligence liability for animals straying onto the highway.
